Nitrogen is the engine of plant growth and the nutrient most often limiting yield in Indian soils, which are largely low in organic matter. It is the core building block of chlorophyll (green colour + photosynthesis), all proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) and is directly responsible for vegetative vigour, tillering/branching, leaf area, and grain protein. A shortfall shows up faster and hits yield harder than almost any other nutrient, which is why India consumes more urea than any other fertiliser.

Potassium is the 'quality and stress' nutrient — it regulates water (stomata), builds stem strength (anti-lodging), improves disease/drought/cold tolerance, and drives sugar/starch transport that determines fruit size, colour, TSS, and grain filling. It is not built into tissue like N/P but activates 60+ enzymes and governs plant health.

Cobalt is essential for the Rhizobium bacteria that fix nitrogen in legume nodules (it is part of vitamin B12/cobalamin needed by the bacteria). It is not proven essential for the plant itself but is vital for legume N-fixation and for grazing animals (B12). Deficiency shows indirectly as poor nodulation/N-fixation in pulses.

Calcium is the cement of cell walls and the regulator of new-tissue growth. It moves only with the transpiration stream, so deficiency hits the newest growth and fruit even when soil Ca is adequate. Responsible for blossom-end rot, tip-burn, and fruit cracking — disorders farmers routinely mistake for disease.

Molybdenum is needed in the tiniest amounts but is essential for two key enzymes: nitrate reductase (converts nitrate to usable N) and nitrogenase (biological N-fixation in legume nodules). Deficiency is worst on ACID soils and shows as N-deficiency-like yellowing plus the classic cauliflower 'whiptail'.

Very dark blue-green leaves, excessive leafiness, soft succulent stems, delayed flowering/maturity, LODGING (falling over) in cereals/sugarcane, and higher pest/disease susceptibility (aphids, borers, blights love lush N-rich tissue). In leafy/veg crops, nitrate accumulation raises food-safety concern.

Nickel is the most recently confirmed essential micronutrient. It is a cofactor of UREASE (which converts urea to usable ammonia) and of hydrogenase in N-fixation. Needed in the tiniest amount; deficiency is extremely rare in field crops but can cause urea toxicity build-up and leaf-tip necrosis.

Phosphorus is the energy currency of the plant (ATP/ADP), drives root development, early establishment, flowering, seed/grain formation and crop maturity. Indian soils are widely P-deficient and P gets 'fixed' (locked) fast, so placement and timing matter more than for any other nutrient.

Copper is a cofactor of photosynthetic and respiratory enzymes and is critical for lignin (stem strength), pollen viability and grain set. Deficiency is uncommon but occurs on sandy, peaty/organic and heavily-limed soils, causing wilting young shoots, twisted tips and poor grain set.

Boron is vital for cell-wall formation, pollen viability, flowering, fruit/seed set and sugar transport. It has the NARROWEST margin between deficiency and toxicity of any nutrient. Deficiency causes hollow stem/browning in cauliflower, fruit cracking, flower drop and poor seed set.

Sulphur is the 4th major nutrient and the #1 hidden deficiency in Indian oilseeds and pulses. It builds sulphur-containing amino acids (cysteine, methionine), proteins, oils and the enzymes of N metabolism. A crop can look N-deficient but actually be S-starved — urea won't fix it.

Silicon is a beneficial (near-essential for rice, sugarcane, other grasses) nutrient that strengthens cell walls, making plants stand erect (anti-lodging), resist pests/diseases (blast, stem borer, BPH) and tolerate drought/salinity. Rice and sugarcane remove huge amounts of Si.

Zinc is the MOST widespread micronutrient deficiency in Indian soils (esp. rice-wheat belt). It is vital for auxin (growth hormone) synthesis, enzyme systems and protein metabolism. Deficiency causes stunting, short internodes, and interveinal chlorosis — 'khaira' in rice.

Iron is essential for chlorophyll synthesis and electron transport in photosynthesis/respiration. Deficiency (iron chlorosis) is very common on calcareous/high-pH soils of India and shows as bright interveinal yellowing of the newest leaves with sharp green veins.

Chlorine (as chloride) is essential in small amounts for the water-splitting step of photosynthesis, osmotic/stomatal regulation and disease suppression. In India, chloride DEFICIENCY is very rare — chloride TOXICITY/salinity is the real, common field problem.

Stop further N immediately; apply extra K (and P) to rebalance and firm tissue; give a light-load stress (controlled irrigation) to slow growth; support/prop lodging-prone crops; increase pest/disease scouting; on next crop, cut N dose and switch to splits.

Magnesium is the CENTRAL ATOM of the chlorophyll molecule — no Mg, no green, no photosynthesis. It also activates many enzymes and helps move phosphorus. Deficiency shows as classic interveinal yellowing of older leaves with green veins.

Pale yellow-green crop, poor/late tillering, thin stand; older leaves yellow from tip along midrib then dry; short plants, small panicles, fewer filled grains. Whole-field paleness after transplanting shock or on sandy/leached bunds.

Manganese activates the water-splitting step of photosynthesis (oxygen evolution) and many enzymes. Deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis of younger leaves with grey/brown flecks; common on high-pH, sandy and heavily-limed soils.
Pale green overall, older-leaf yellowing; because it is a legume, true N-hunger often signals POOR NODULATION (no Rhizobium) rather than soil N shortage — check root nodules before piling on urea.
2% urea (20 g/L) sprayed on foliage for FAST rescue of visible deficiency, at flowering, or when soil is dry/cold and roots can't take up N. Fastest greening but supplements, not replaces, soil N.
Textbook V-shaped yellowing from the TIP of lower leaves along the midrib; stalks thin, sometimes reddish/purple; poor cob fill, tip barrenness. The clearest N-deficiency picture of all crops.
Dissolve water-soluble N (urea, 19:19:19, KNO3) and deliver through drip in small frequent doses. Highest use-efficiency; standard for vegetables, polyhouse capsicum/cucumber, sugarcane drip.

N builds chlorophyll and the Rubisco enzyme that fixes CO2. Adequate N = dark green leaves, large leaf area, high photosynthetic rate. Deficient plants are pale and photosynthesise poorly.
Full-dose basal urea (instead of splits), broadcasting on dry/hot surface without incorporation, and wrong timing all cause huge volatilisation/leaching losses so little reaches the plant.
Never broadcast on dry/hot soil surface (heavy ammonia loss) — incorporate or irrigate. Do not exceed 2% foliar (leaf scorch). Do not mix urea foliar with strongly alkaline products.
Even spreading over the field, then incorporate/irrigate. Use for basal N and large-area top-dressing in cereals. Never leave urea on dry hot surface — wash in to avoid ammonia loss.
Use SOP instead of MOP on sensitive/saline situations; leach salts with good water; improve drainage; gypsum for sodic soils; choose tolerant crops/varieties; test irrigation water.
Distinct yellowing (chlorosis) of lower/older leaves starting from the leaf TIP and moving down the midrib in a V-shape (classic in maize/paddy); fewer tillers/branches, thin stand.
Highest single-nutrient yield response in most Indian crops. Determines number of tillers/ears, grains per ear, leaf area duration and thus total dry-matter and economic yield.
Ni deficiency in Indian field crops is essentially theoretical/very rare; soils normally supply enough. Most relevant to research and to some perennial/nut crops abroad.

Avoid Ni-contaminated inputs/sludge; lime acid soils to reduce Ni availability; add organic matter; apply Fe/Zn; phytoremediation on contaminated land.
